Photo by CARLOS JASSO / Getty Images Article content Thousands of people gathered in central London late Monday to hold a vigil for black academic Jason Arday, blaming racism and relentless media pressure for his death last week. Sign In or Create an Account or View more offers Article content The vigil in Trafalgar Square came as the head of Cambridge university Monday condemned a “racist feeding frenzy” prompted by plagiarism claims against Arday. Article content Article content Arday, who became Cambridge’s youngest-ever black professor when he was appointed in 2023, was found dead Friday aged 41, after mounting accusations he had plagiarized parts of his doctoral thesis and exaggerated some of his personal life achievements. Article content Article content Chris Smith, the University of Cambridge’s chancellor, told the BBC he believed it was important for such claims to be “rigorously investigated.” Article content NP Posted Get a dash of perspective along with the trending news of the day in a very readable format. Article content But amid a media storm surrounding the accusations, Smith added it was right to “refuse to join in a racist feeding frenzy over a particular academic.” Article content Arday, who was diagnosed with autism and other developmental difficulties as a child, had disputed the allegations against him. Article content But he said in a public resignation letter on Aug. 5 that he had “reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.” Article content The cause of his death has not been made public, with police saying only it was not suspicious and they were preparing a file for a coroner. Article content Arday’s family did not attend the vigil, but issued a statement that was read to the crowd, thanking supporters for their “love, support, and grief.” Article content “The public cruelty Jason was subjected to was too much for any man to bear,” they said, describing Arday as a “selfless and gentle soul.” Article content “His achievements were great, and we do not want misrepresentations about his character to overshadow them,” the family said. Article content Article content His friend Jonathan Miller, deputy head of Froebel College, University of Roehampton, said he was grateful so many turned out to honour Arday. Article content “It’s just crying shame that brilliant man has felt that he had nowhere to turn,” Miller told AFP. Article content MP Diane Abbott, the first black woman ever elected to the U.K. parliament, told the rally, organized by campaign group Stand Up To Racism, that she saw Arday a week ago. Article content “He felt he had no choice but to resign. And he must have felt that if he resigned, the attacks on him would stop. But, in fact, they got even worse from his resignation to his suicide last week,” she said. “It wasn’t just a campaign against the professor. It was a campaign against all of us.” Article content Stand Up To Racism said some 30,000 people attended Monday’s rally, although AFP could not immediately confirm the figure. Article content Many were dressed in black, carrying roses and sunflowers as well as banners saying “Rest in power Professor Jason Arday.” Article content Claire Lynch, 69, a retired dyslexia teacher, told AFP she had been “horrified” by what had happened to Arday, saying he had been “hounded.” Advertisement 1 This advertisement has not loaded yet. Article content “I spent a lot of my life teaching my pupils that they could do anything, if they put their mind to it. And to see someone brought down who was doing exactly that — he would have been someone I was holding up as an example.” Article content Alex Pascall, 89, said Arday’s death should serve as a “wake-up” call, saying it was “time for these type of things to stop.” Article content A separate, smaller vigil was also held in Cambridge on Monday. Article content An online fundraising page created by racial equality campaigner Patrick Vernon to support Arday’s family had raised over £174,000 ($327,000) by Monday evening. Article content Separately, a petition demanding an immediate public inquiry into the media coverage of Arday had gathered over 90,000 signatures late Monday including from Abbott and Green Party leader Zack Polanski. Article content Addressed to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the petition posted by activist group Good Law Project claimed Arday’s death was the result of “press harassment.” Article content Downing Street declined to say whether any inquiry was planned, repeating Burnham’s comments on Saturday that it was a time for “reflection.” Article content The petition said Arday’s death came after “two weeks of relentless harassment,” stressing that “racism lay at the heart of this story.” Article content Article content The university is also facing questions over its handling of the allegations and its treatment of Arday. Article content Last week, before the announcement of Arday’s death, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice announced an investigation into the circumstances of his appointment and his time working at the university. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Senator Jacqui Lambie is responsible for 6% of total swearing in parliament, at a rate of 406 swear words per million words spoken – more than 19 times the average. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images The Crunch Australian politics Potty-mouthed MPs ranked as Australian parliament sets new swearing record One serial swearing offender, Jacqui Lambie, says it wouldn’t be an Australian parliament ‘without a few swear words thrown in’ Want to get more charts in your inbox every fortnight? Sign up for The Crunch here Hannah Schuller , Josh Butler and Andy Ball Sun 22 Nov 2026 09.00 EST Last modified on Sun 22 Nov 2026 15.31 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google When Liberal MP Garth Hamilton stormed out of parliament in June, slamming his hands on his desk and calling out “fucking bullshit”, the speaker of the house, Milton Dick, called it “a new low” in federal politics. Dick may have been on to something. New analysis from Guardian Australia has found profanity and foul language has risen significantly in Australia’s parliament over the past 20 years, with some of today’s most prominent politicians among the chief culprits for swearing. Before the year is even out, 2026 is the worst year on record for the use of swear words and language deemed “unparliamentary”. That number has risen by 78% since 2006. Analysis of Hansard debate and procedure records has found that per million words spoken in parliament this year, approximately 37 have been profane – ranging from milder (“bloody”, “damn” and “crap”) to language considered strong, or even extreme. Line chart showing swear words per million words spoken in the Australian parliament from 2006 to 2026. The rate fluctuates but trends upwards, rising from about 16 in 2006 to a peak of 37 in 2026, with a low of around 12 in 2009. A dotted trend line highlights the overall increase. While entitled to “parle hard”, language deemed unparliamentary by the speaker or Senate president is required to be withdrawn, or else MPs face ejection from the chamber. So why bother? Beyond the impact of pushing against regulation and etiquette, there is something to be said for the currency that outbursts gain when clipped and shared online – recently demonstrated by Greens senator Peter Whish-Wilson, who called for the country to “wake the fuck up” to One Nation’s use of social media algorithms in June. But despite the politicians reaching for profanities at a record rate, Dick – the Labor MP who has been speaker of the house since 2022 – said he felt the tone and tenor of debate in parliament has gotten better in his time in the chair. “Debate is fierce and strong and, apart from a few incidents, it has improved,” he said. “Maybe it hasn’t appeared so because of the volume [of swearing], but when you analyse the words used … there are outbreaks of course, but I believe in everyone showing respect.” And, to be fair, most of parliament’s most swear-y politicians are in the Senate, not the house. An oral tradition Described as “the great Australian adjective” in 1894 by the Bulletin magazine, “bloody” appears to have suffered no fall from grace in the subsequent years, serving as the most commonly used swear word in parliament. Along with “damn”, “crap” and “bugger”, mild curses constitute 92% of all recorded bad language, with more severe terms such as “prick”, “shit” and “piss” used more sparingly. Excluded from this figure are rare cases of colourful and creative terms that have been called for withdrawal. Harnessing the speaker’s unilateral power to flag unacceptable language, terms such as “bin chickens – used by Julian Hill, the MP for Bruce, in 2022 to describe the opposition in the house – have been ruled as unparliamentary. Swearing and swearing allegiance Much of this potty-talk comes from the Senate, which since 2006 has seen a 177% increase in the use of bad language. Among active parliamentary participants (those who have spoken at least 100,000 words in this period), Bill Heffernan was the lead offender. Despite speaking just 141,000 words between 2006 and 2016, the former Liberal senator had an expletive use-rate of 877 per million words spoken, 43 times the rate of all other parliamentarians. Stacked bar chart showing swear words per million words spoken in the Australian parliament, 2006–2026. Bill Heffernan leads with 877.2, followed by Jacqui Lambie (406.3), Derryn Hinch (398.4), Glenn Sterle (294.3), Russell Matheson (206.9), David Shoebridge (179.5), Pauline Hanson (169.5), Jordon Steele-John (167.9) and Steph Hodgins-May (161.6). Mild swear words make up most of each total, with smaller contributions from strong and extreme language. Only politicians who spoke more than 100,000 words are included. Jacqui Lambie is the second-most sweary politician, responsible for 6% of total swearing in parliament at a rate of 406 per million words spoken – more than 19 times the average. But, like most of the politicians on this list, Lambie’s swearing is overwhelmingly mild – mostly words like “crap” or “bloody”. “I try really hard not to swear, especially in the Senate chamber. It upsets my mum, she doesn’t even like me saying ‘bloody’,” Lambie said when we came to her with the statistics. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Fortnightly Sign up to The Crunch Our data journalists showcase the most important charts and dataviz from the Guardian and around the web, free every fortnight after newsletter promotion “It’s important to be respectful. But I am a straight shooter and sometimes things are just crap – and it’s hard not to say so. I don’t think it would be an Australian parliament without a few swear words thrown in.” Not all occurrences of swearing in parliamentary records are “own-use” or, rather, swearing with intent. Quotes, such as reading out abuse a politician has received, or a quote from a document, account for some of it. However, when excluding these cases our analysis shows that own-use swearing in parliament has nearly tripled over the last 20 years, from 6.4 per million words in 2006-9 to 18.9 in 2022-5. Line chart showing the three-year rolling rate of politicians’ own-use swearing per million words spoken in the Australian parliament, by party, from 2008 to 2026. One Nation peaks at about 175 in 2024 before falling to 110 in 2026. The Greens rise unevenly, reaching nearly 100 in 2026. Independents peak at about 80 in 2017 before declining sharply. Labor and Liberal rates remain below 15 throughout, while the Nationals reach about 24 in 2026. Broken down by party, One Nation are the worst offenders, swearing for the sake of it at 7.4 times the rate of Labor – perhaps unsurprising, given that the party leader, Pauline Hanson, ranks fourth among discursively active politicians for use of foul language. Dick said he had strived to improve the tone of discussion in parliament, believing that greater diversity in politics and in the chamber – with more women, more First Nations MPs and people from multicultural backgrounds – had also changed dynamics of debate. Asked about recent heated moments in parliament, he said he recalled only two major moments in the lower house in recent years: Hamilton’s June storm-out and fellow Liberal MP Dan Tehan’s demand to “cut the crap” in August. “I want to ensure, among our people and our democracy, that we fight hard to disagree more civilly … But I’m a big believer in upholding traditions and standards. When things get a bit heated, I’ll take firm action,” Dick said. Notes on the analysis Politicians’ speeches from both houses of parliament were analysed for the years 2006 to 2026. For each speech, the number of swearwords were counted using the these categories: Mild: bloody, damn, crap, bugger, bastard, bulldust, arse, mongrel, boofhead, bollocks Strong: prick, shit, bullshit, piss, piss off, dickhead, arsehole, shithouse, wanker Extreme: fucking, cunt, fuck, fuck off, fucker, fucked, motherfucker To control for politicians’ tenure length and verbosity affecting swearing totals, swearing numbers were converted to a rate per million words by dividing the total swearwords by the total number of words spoken for that politician in that year, or for the total time period. To separate swearing in a politician’s own voice from quotes, idioms and literal uses, an LLM was used to read the speech text surrounding each swearword and sort these into categories. A random sample of the results were manually checked, to achieve an agreement of 97% on whether a use was the speaker’s own. Therefore these figures are approximate.
